q: If your page uses HTTPS, the user cannot read the requests in their own Network tab.
why: No. HTTPS protects the road between the browser and the server from people in the middle. The user is on the browser side, so they see the plain request and answer.

q: A secret API key is in your browser JavaScript. Where can a visitor read it?
options: In the Network tab headers and in the page code
Nowhere, because browser code is private
Only if they hack your database
why: Browser code and the requests it makes are on the user's machine. The key is visible in the Network tab and in the bundle file. A key that was ever public must be replaced.

q: Which of these really protect an API that the frontend calls?
options: Check the login and the permission on the server for every request
Call the third party from your server so the key stays there
why: Server checks, a server-side proxy and a rate limit work. Base64 is only another way to write the same text, and one call to atob() undoes it.

q: A cookie is marked HttpOnly. What does that stop?
options: JavaScript on the page reading the cookie, such as an XSS script
The user seeing the cookie in DevTools
The cookie being sent to the server
why: HttpOnly keeps scripts away from the cookie. The user can still see their own cookie in DevTools, and a copied cookie still works until the session ends.

q: Put the checks of a safe proxy route in the right order.
items: Check that the user is logged in
Call the third party with the key
Send back only the fields the screen needs
why: Do the cheap checks first. Do not spend a paid third party call, or use your key, for someone who is not logged in or who is over the limit.

q: What is the name of the browser tool, opened with F12, where the user can read every request and answer? (two words)
why: The Network tab lists the requests with their headers, bodies, answers and timing. You cannot hide a request from it.
